t: Ottoman Turkish was the Turkish of the empire’s court, poetry and administration, so full of Arabic and Persian that words from them made up as much as 88% of its vocabulary.
It was largely unintelligible to rural Turks, who spoke kaba Türkçe, “rough Turkish”, with far fewer loanwords, the basis of modern standard Turkish.
In 1928, under Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, the Republic of Turkey replaced the Perso-Arabic script with an extended Latin alphabet and began replacing Arabic and Persian loanwords with Turkish ones.
dyk: The same speaker could use two languages for one thing: a scribe would write the Arabic word asel for honey in a document, but would ask for it by the Turkish word bal when buying it.
ev: Old Ottoman Turkish, almost identical with the Turkish of the Seljuks and the Anatolian beyliks, is the language of the young Ottoman state
Classical Ottoman Turkish becomes the language of poetry and administration, as it remains until the Tanzimat
In the Tanzimat era the language comes to be called “Ottoman”, lisân-ı Osmânî or Osmanlıca
New Ottoman Turkish begins to take shape under the influence of journalism and Western-oriented literature
Atatürk’s reforms replace the Perso-Arabic script with an extended Latin alphabet and begin replacing Arabic and Persian loanwords
Ottoman Turkish is still at least partly intelligible to speakers of the Turkish of the day
Turkey’s Education Council decides that Ottoman Turkish should be taught in Islamic high schools and as an elective in other schools

f.family: Turkic: the standardised register of the Turkish language in the Ottoman Empire; its oldest stage was almost identical with the Turkish of the Seljuk empire and the Anatolian beyliks
f.script: the Ottoman Turkish alphabet (elifbâ), a variant of the Perso-Arabic script, until 1928; Armenians, Greeks and Jews sometimes wrote it in the Armenian and Greek scripts and the Rashi script of Hebrew (Karamanli Turkish in Greek letters)
f.earliest: Old Ottoman Turkish, used until the 16th century, almost identical with the Turkish of the Seljuk empire and the Anatolian beyliks and often counted as part of Old Anatolian Turkish
f.status: no longer used: in 1928 the Republic of Turkey replaced its script with an extended Latin alphabet and began replacing its Arabic and Persian loanwords with Turkish ones; its successor is modern Turkish; since a 2014 decision it is taught in Islamic high schools and as an elective in other schools
